meanings.note: Aparecer na frente means to show up in the lead in election tallies.

examples.trans: The candidate appears in the lead.
He showed up at the meeting.

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.

examples.trans: He is in the meeting.
She stays on her phone.

meanings.note: Used in na frente de (in front of someone).

examples.text: Não grita na frente dos outros!
examples.trans: Don't shout in front of everyone else!

examples.text: Te espero na frente da sala.
examples.trans: I'll wait for you in front of the room.

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.

examples.trans: It’s a marketing meeting.
I’m in finance.

meanings.note: Used for individual ballots and election totals such as votos válidos (valid votes).

examples.trans: He got many votes.
We counted the valid votes.

meanings.note: In Brazilian elections, votos válidos exclude blank and null ballots.

examples.text: Ele tem metade dos votos válidos.
examples.trans: He has half of the valid votes.
This ticket is still valid.

meanings.note: Acabou o seu tempo is the standard phrase for 'Your time is up.'

examples.trans: Your time is up.
The meeting has already ended.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: What is your job title?
Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.

examples.trans: I’m going to the meeting.
Aren’t you going?

meanings.note: Sair daqui means to get out of here.

examples.trans: Let's get out of here now.
She left earlier today.

meanings.note: Contraction of de + aqui.

examples.text: A dor pega daqui até o pescoço.
examples.trans: The pain goes from here up to my neck.
We are close to here.

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.

examples.trans: I’m in finance.
I’m not going.

meanings.note: Takes a direct object in Portuguese without a preposition for 'for'.

examples.trans: I am looking for an apartment.
She is looking for a two-bedroom place.

meanings.note: Used for plane, bus, or train tickets when traveling.

examples.trans: I am going to look for a ticket to Portugal.
Did you already buy the ticket?

meanings.note: Full form of informal pra; introduces purpose before an infinitive or direction.

examples.trans: I have a lot to sort out.
Look in there.

meanings.note: With ir, ir embora means to leave or go away (here euphemistically for passing on).

examples.text: Mas tá indo embora na verdade.
examples.trans: But she is leaving in fact.
I need to leave now.

meanings.note: Used for delivering food (entregar comida) or handing in work.

examples.trans: I deliver food by motorcycle.
I already handed in the report.

meanings.note: Everyday noun for food or prepared meals, as in entregar comida (to deliver food).

examples.trans: I deliver food in the city.

examples.text: A comida aqui é muito boa.
examples.trans: The food here is very good.

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.

examples.trans: No, I’m not going.
Aren’t you going?

meanings.note: Covers knowing facts or finding out information.

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.
Do you know the answer?

meanings.note: A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?
Are you in finance?

cuidar.gloss: to take care of; look after

meanings.en: to take care of; look after
meanings.note: Takes the preposition de before the person or thing cared for: cuidar de velhos.

examples.text: Você cuida de velhos muito bem.
examples.trans: You take care of old people very well.
Who is going to take care of this?

meanings.note: Can be an adjective (old) or a plural noun os velhos referring colloquially to elderly people.

examples.text: Você cuida de velhos muito bem.
examples.trans: You take care of old people very well.

examples.text: Meu avô conhece os velhos do bairro.
examples.trans: My grandfather knows the old folks in the neighborhood.

meanings.note: Irregular past eu fiz (I made/did); não tem o que fazer means having nothing to do.

examples.text: Ela não tem o que fazer agora.
examples.trans: She has nothing to do now.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

meanings.note: Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.

examples.trans: What is this, man?
That slows everyone else down.

meanings.note: Conditional eu gostaria softens a refusal (I would like to, but...).

examples.trans: I would like to, but I have work.
I really like this team.

meanings.note: Polite everyday term for an older adult or senior citizen.

examples.text: Eu gosto de cuidar de idoso.
examples.trans: I like taking care of the elderly.

examples.text: O ônibus tem assento para idosos.
examples.trans: The bus has seats for seniors.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.
There are some good numbers.

meanings.note: Masculine noun despite ending in -a.

examples.text: Ficar só sentado é um problema.
examples.trans: Staying seated all the time is a problem.
Let's solve this problem now.

meanings.note: Placed after a singular noun (problema nenhum) for emphatic negation: no problem at all.

examples.trans: There is no problem at all.

examples.text: Não tenho nenhum jeito de sair.
examples.trans: I have no way at all to leave.

meanings.note: From virar (to turn); used in sports and elections when the trailing side takes the lead.

examples.trans: It was a historic turnaround.
The comeback happened at the end.

meanings.note: Assumir a liderança means to take the lead.

examples.trans: Lula takes the lead now.
She took over the new position.

meanings.note: Assumir a liderança and voltar à liderança are standard election-night phrases for taking the lead.

examples.trans: The candidate took the lead.

examples.text: Ela voltou à liderança na pesquisa.
examples.trans: She returned to the lead in the poll.

meanings.note: Used enthusiastically in gerund (estou amando) for loving an experience right now.

examples.trans: I am loving us chatting.
They love traveling by car.

meanings.note: Demonstrative determiner; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese esse commonly covers both this near me and that just mentioned.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

examples.text: Vou ficar sentado esse tempo inteiro.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay seated that whole time.

meanings.note: Stressed on the final -ís; o país often refers to Brazil in domestic news and conversation.

examples.trans: I love this country.

examples.text: Criança é o futuro do país.
examples.trans: Children are the future of the country.

meanings.note: Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.
What is this, man?

meanings.note: Introduces a condition; triggers future subjunctive when referring to a possible future action (se vocês olharem).

examples.text: Se eu vou entrar, você vai também.
examples.trans: If I'm going in, you're going too.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Reflexive se mudar para means to relocate or move to a new place.

examples.text: A gente tem que se mudar para o interior.
examples.trans: We have to move to the countryside.
He changed his mind.

meanings.note: In Brazil, o interior means towns and rural areas outside the state capitals and coast.

examples.text: A gente quer se mudar para o interior.
examples.trans: We want to move to the countryside.
My parents live in the countryside.

meanings.note: Used standalone in speech to mean of course / obviously.

examples.trans: I will need help, of course.
The explanation was very clear.

meanings.note: Followed by an infinitive for your own wish (quero saber) or que + subjunctive for someone else (quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.
Is that what you want?

meanings.note: Ter filho means to have children; plural filhos covers sons or children in general.

examples.text: Claro que eu quero ter filho.
examples.trans: Of course I want to have children.
They have two children.

meanings.note: Grammatically feminine whether referring to a boy, a girl, or children in general.

examples.text: Criança é o futuro do país.
examples.trans: Children are the future of the country.
The kids are playing.

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.

examples.trans: I’m in finance.
It’s a marketing meeting.

meanings.note: O futuro do país is a classic civic phrase for the nation's future.

examples.text: Criança é o futuro do país.
examples.trans: Children are the future of the country.
We think about our future.

meanings.note: In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.

examples.trans: See you later!
See you later. Thanks!

meanings.note: In the farewell até logo it anticipates meeting again. This is the time adverb, not a short form for a company logo.

examples.trans: See you later!
I’ll go to the meeting soon.
